title: Which primes make the HCF and the LCM?
description: Two numbers are given as products of primes. The smaller count of each prime gives the highest common factor and the larger count gives the lowest common multiple, first as primes and then as numbers. Keeko doubts this and says the lowest common multiple takes only the primes in both numbers.
teaching_notes: One idea: read the highest common factor and the lowest common multiple straight from the prime counts, the smaller count for the first and the larger count for the second. Watch for students who build the lowest common multiple from the shared primes only.

source: Find the HCF and LCM of 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 and 2 × 3 × 3 × 7, giving the answers as prime factorisations and as numbers.
video_script.why: The child can find a highest common factor and a lowest common multiple from prime counts and now does it for numbers given only as primes.
video_script.substitution: Count each prime in both numbers, take the smaller count for the highest common factor and the larger count for the lowest common multiple.
video_script.anchor: The two products of primes written one under the other, with the same primes in the same columns.
video_script.wrong_answer: the lowest common multiple takes only the primes in both numbers
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko builds the lowest common multiple from two and three only, which gives six, but six is smaller than sixty and cannot be a multiple of it.
video_script.payoff_line: The highest common factor is six and the lowest common multiple is one thousand two hundred sixty

final_answer.spoken: the highest common factor is two times three, which is six, and the lowest common multiple is two times two times three times three times five times seven, which is one thousand two hundred sixty

never_show: 6 as the lowest common multiple, marked right
maths_rules: primes: 2, 3, 5, 7; counts in the first and second number: 2 has 2 and 1, 3 has 1 and 2, 5 has 1 and 0, 7 has 0 and 1
smaller counts: 2 once, 3 once, so HCF = 2 × 3 = 6
larger counts: 2 twice, 3 twice, 5 once, 7 once, so LCM = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 × 7 = 4 × 9 × 35 = 1260
slip: 2 × 3 = 6 is less than 60, so it cannot be a multiple of 60
video_script.design: One idea: the smaller prime counts give the highest common factor and the larger counts give the lowest common multiple. The two products of primes stay on the board.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The first number is two times two times three times five.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The second number is two times three times three times seven.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The largest number that divides both numbers is called their highest common factor.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>The smallest number that is a multiple of both is called their lowest common multiple. Which primes make each of them?

beats.on_screen: the two products of primes and the two boxes stay on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: the two products of primes lined up in columns, one column for each prime; the number of times each prime appears is written under it

marks.m1: the two products are lined up with one column for each prime
marks.m2: the number of times each prime appears is written under it

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>A prime can appear more than once in a number. We line up the same primes in columns.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Then we count how many times each prime appears in each number.

marks.m1: the given line is written in the working band

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, two times two times three times five, and two times three times three times seven.

beats.on_screen: To find: HCF and LCM, as primes and as numbers

marks.m1: the find line is written under the given line

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to find the highest common factor and the lowest common multiple, as primes and as numbers.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: primes 2, 3, 5, 7. Counts in the two numbers: 2 has 2 and 1; 3 has 1 and 2; 5 has 1 and 0; 7 has 0 and 1

marks.m1: the primes 2, 3, 5 and 7 are written in a row
marks.m2: the counts 2 and 1 are written under 2, and 1 and 2 under 3
marks.m3: the counts 1 and 0 are written under 5, and 0 and 1 under 7

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, the primes are two, three, five and seven.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Two appears twice in the first number and once in the second. Three appears once and then twice.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Five appears only in the first number. Seven appears only in the second.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: smaller counts: 2 once, 3 once. HCF = 2 × 3 = 6

marks.m1: the smaller count of each prime is lit

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, for the highest common factor we take the smaller count of each prime. That is two once and three once, while five and seven count zero.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Two times three is six.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: larger counts: 2 twice, 3 twice, 5 once, 7 once. LCM = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 × 7 = 4 × 9 × 35 = 1260

marks.m1: the larger count of each prime is lit

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, for the lowest common multiple we take the larger count of each prime. That is two twice, three twice, five once and seven once.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>We multiply them all together.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Four times nine is thirty six, and thirty six times thirty five is one thousand two hundred sixty.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, the two numbers are sixty and one hundred twenty six.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Six goes into sixty ten times, and into one hundred twenty six twenty one times.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Twenty one times sixty is one thousand two hundred sixty. Ten times one hundred twenty six is the same.

marks.m3: the value 1260 is written beside the LCM

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>The highest common factor is two times three, which is six.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The lowest common multiple is two times two times three times three times five times seven.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The highest common factor is six and the lowest common multiple is one thousand two hundred sixty.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the columns of primes
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: LCM = 2 × 3 = 6; 6 is set beside 60 and is smaller; the bubble is struck out and 5 and 7 are added back

marks.m1: Keeko's bubble shows the LCM built from 2 and 3 only
marks.m2: 6 is set beside the first number 60 and is smaller
marks.m4: 5 and 7 are added back into the product

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks the lowest common multiple takes only the primes in both numbers. That gives two times three, which is six.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>But the first number is sixty, and a multiple of sixty cannot be as small as six.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>A multiple of a number must hold every prime of that number.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>That is why five and seven must come in too.
